#4782. The 9 Best Sweaters for Men, Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

From classic cotton crews to cozy cashmere, every knit is here.

I’LL ADMIT IT: sweaters are my kryptonite. Long before I was a style editor, they were my secret weapon. In my early twenties, I realized that a well-cut knit could elevate a look more effortlessly than any blazer or jacket. I’ve worn them through newsroom winters, weekend getaways, and way too many cold subway commutes to count. Growing up, I’d watch Pharrell Williams turn a simple crewneck into a statement, marvel at Andre 3000’s fearless layering, and admire A$AP Rocky’s ability to make a chunky sweater feel cool. Those moments have stuck with me, teaching me that style isn’t about what you wear but how you wear it. Sweaters became my canvas—and they still are, whether I’m braving the elements or dressing to impress.

Since 2020, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested more than 50 styles—crewnecks, cable knits, turtlenecks—to find the ones that actually deliver. Sweaters are also one of my go-to holiday gifts since they’re practical and available at just about every price point. Ahead, you’ll find our top picks that check every box, whether you’re shopping for yourself or grabbing dad a new knit for the season.

I’ve been testing men’s sweaters since 2020, so as you can imagine, I’ve worn more than I can count. Polo Ralph Lauren’s cable-knit has consistently risen above the competition in construction, fit, and timeless style. The brand helped cement the cable-knit as an American preppy classic, and that history shows in the sweater itself. The textured braids and patterns give it depth and richness, elevating even the simplest outfit. You can see and feel the heritage in every stitch—the weight, the structure, the classic lines all signal a piece built to last.

The relaxed fit is a major win for comfort—it offers extra room in the chest, which is perfect if you’ve got bigger pecs (like me, after a few years of lifting). Even without spandex, it layers beautifully over a button-up without stretching out or losing its shape. During testing, I wore it over a crisp white dress shirt for a dinner party, under a blazer for a Zoom meeting, and casually with joggers on a morning matcha latte run. The fabric feels soft against the skin but maintains structure. It never made me break a sweat, and kept me cozy in temps in the high 50s. I’ve washed mine over six times, and the sweater still looks and fits like new.

I also love how it pairs seamlessly with a variety of pants—tailored trousers, jeans, and casual sweats all work. And of course, that unmistakable Ralph Lauren heritage baked in, giving a sense of legacy that many sweaters lack. One thing to keep in mind: it comes with a premium price tag, which might be a barrier, only if you’re looking for a budget-friendly option that won’t exude as much style.

Amazon Essentials offers everything from the best men’s basics to sharp sweaters, and this one’s proof that affordable doesn’t mean cheaply made. This V-neck style is breathable in the winter, easy to layer, and feels surprisingly premium for the price. Our editors wore it under blazers and sport coats, and then over a crisp shirt with the collar peeking. (Don’t wear it with a T-shirt unless you’re going for a laid-back look). The regular fit is relaxed–but-not-boxy, and forgiving if you’ve just had a burger.

The 100 percent cotton knit feels soft against the skin with just the right amount of stretch, so there’s no restriction when I raise my arms or reach for my coffee. Given its price, you’d think it would become dingy after a few wears or washes, but that’s not the case. Despite months of wear and multiple wash cycles, it held its shape without fading or pilling. Bonus: it comes in a range of colors and argyle prints, so you can stock up and keep your office fits in rotation.

If outdoor running is part of your winter routine, you should consider Vuori’s Performance Crew. It’s designed with both comfort and functionality in mind. Made from a stretchy, moisture-wicking fabric, it keeps you dry and moves with you, whether you’re running errands or working up a sweat. The brand’s signature DreamKnit fabric feels like velvet and won’t overheat you when layered over a lightweight T-shirt or tank top. It's by far the smoothest, most buttery-soft fabric we’ve ever tested. With a modern athletic fit, the cut follows the natural shape of your body without being too tight or loose. You still have the freedom of movement while still looking put-together, so it’s perfect for intense workouts and casual wear.

A good cashmere sweater feels like wrapping yourself in a cloud, and Naadam’s version is one that our style team can’t get enough of. The first time I pulled it on, I understood why: it’s ridiculously soft—way softer than regular wool so it feels amazing against my skin without any itching. It’s lightweight too, so you don’t overheat when the radiator’s on full blast, but still warm enough for windy commutes.

After a few wears, I noticed it never lost its shape and didn’t pill as fast as cheaper cashmere sweaters I’ve tested (a small miracle at this price). Keep in mind: cashmere is delicate, so this one requires more care than cotton or polyester sweaters. I’m also a fan of how many colors they offer, including cobalt and tangerine that really stand out without being loud. For guys with athletic builds, it’s the perfect cut. It skims your frame just right, showing off your shoulders and giving your biceps a little spotlight. Just note: sizes do run small, so if you’re between sizes, go up.

I’ve tested a bunch of budget knits, but this one from Uniqlo punches way above its price tag. The cotton-blend fabric feels soft straight out of the package and has a tight ribbed construction that keeps its shape after a dozen washes, and somehow still looks brand new. Although it doesn’t have the weight or the luxe feel of higher-end knits, I’ve worn this for months and found no fading, stretching, or weird pilling.

The synthetic blend gives it that smooth, premium hand-feel with a bit of stretch, so you can reach, twist, and move without feeling boxed in. I also love how the fit strikes that sweet spot between tailored and relaxed—it skims the body without clinging, which makes it look sharp enough for the office but laid-back enough for Sunday coffee runs. The ribbing on the collar keeps it in shape and adds a subtle texture, providing a durable and neat finish. And since it’s machine washable, you can toss it in with your regular laundry and forget about dry cleaning.

I’ve always loved turtleneck sweaters—they’re dressier and provide more coverage than your standard crewneck. But if you’re on the shorter or leaner side, a full turtleneck can sometimes feel like too much fabric stacked around your neck. Suitsupply’s roll neck solves that problem perfectly. It delivers the same refined look and warmth of a turtleneck, just with less bulk so you don’t need a scarf. I found it especially handy during the freezing winter mornings. The merino wool breathes surprisingly well, so I didn’t overheat when layering it under a blazer or waiting for the train in a muggy subway station.

You can skip a trip to the dry cleaners because the fabric is tough enough to handle a spin in the washer and come out looking sharp with zero shrinkage or sagging. Plus, it’s odor-resistant, so I stayed fresh from my morning commute through my evening dinner. What I love the most is the versatility. Thanks to its minimalistic look, I’ve layered it under everything from a bomber jacket for errands to a tailored suit for a fancy holiday party. Whether you’re going for laid-back or dress-to-impress, this turtleneck fits the bill perfectly. The slim fit is clean but not constricting—enough to streamline my upper body without being tight, and yes, it gives the pecs a nice little lift. Guys with bigger chests or arms may have to size up for a comfortable fit.

This ribbed crew is one of those pieces that just feels right from the first wear. It’s made from a richly textured cotton rib that gives it some real weight—thicker than your average knit but never stiff or bulky. The texture adds that broken-in look while the classic fit keeps things clean and flattering. It sits close to the body without squeezing you, which makes it great for guys with broader shoulders who want structure, and it gives slimmer builds a sharper, more defined shape. It drapes cleanly through the shoulders and arms, and has just enough give whether you’re layering it under a jacket or reaching for something on a shelf.

What really sets it apart from other sweaters is the feel—it’s got that hearty, hand-knit texture you usually only get from a vintage find, but it wears lighter and breathes better than heavy wool. After its first wash, the ribbing softened up so much we wanted to wear it three days in a row. The look lands somewhere between rugged fisherman and clean-cut. Yeah, it’s not cheap, but the rich construction, flattering fit, and durability make it worth the investment.

If you’re going to wear a sweater, make sure it’s in a classic color that won’t feel dated after one season. This style comes in a nice red or grey that are bold enough to stand out but not overwhelming that you’ll regret it in photos later. It plays well with dressier trousers for a dinner or intimate gathering. The unique ribbing along the sides, neckline, and hem gives it some nice texture, while the standard fit hits that sweet spot between relaxed and put-together. It might feel a bit boxy if you prefer a more tailored, close-to-the-body look.

The merino wool and nylon fabric blend feels sturdy but not stiff—it’s thick enough to keep you warm on chilly mornings but breathable once you’re indoors. One of our testers even wore it on a coffee run and didn’t break a sweat under a jacket. It’s got just the right amount of stretch too, so you can move around without feeling like you're trapped in a knit straitjacket. The vibe is rugged but still polished, which means it works just as well with jeans and clean sneakers, as well as with tailored trousers and loafers.

I’ve been wearing this cashmere quarter-zip from Quince for a few weeks now, and it’s one of those sweaters that makes you realize how nice cashmere can actually feel. The fisherman rib knit gives it real heft and structure, so it feels premium the second you pull it on. This one is made from Mongolian cashmere, which has longer, finer fibers, so it's ten times softer and more durable. You’re basically getting that luxury feel for a budget-friendly price point. It has a classic fit but is trim enough that it doesn’t bunch up when you sit or layer it under a coat or over a button-down.

I wore this during New York City’s shoulder season, and it regulated temperature really well. I never got hot walking to work or felt chilly when the office AC kicked on. The fabric breathes better than most wool sweaters I’ve tested, and it never got that itchy, fuzzy feeling that cashmere can sometimes pick up after a few wears. Plus, the quarter-zip collar gives it versatility, too: zipped up, it looks sharp for the office; unzipped, it leans casual for the weekend. You can choose from a range of easy-to-wear neutral tones; think navy, black, and charcoal, which all pair effortlessly with chinos or dark jeans.

Look for high-quality materials that ensure warmth, comfort, and longevity. By understanding what each fabric brings to the table, you can select the sweater that fits both your lifestyle and your wardrobe goals. Here’s a closer look at what you can expect from the most common options:

Cashmere is the gold standard for softness and luxury. It’s made from the undercoat of cashmere goats, resulting in an ultra-fine, buttery fabric. Expect it to feel lightweight yet warm, perfect for layering without adding bulk. Cashmere sweaters often have a higher price tag, but their timeless appeal and plush feel make them a worthwhile investment. Just remember: cashmere requires delicate care, like handwashing or dry cleaning, to maintain its softness.

Merino wool is a performance powerhouse. Derived from Merino sheep, this wool is fine, soft, and naturally moisture-wicking, making it ideal for regulating body temperature. Merino wool sweaters keep you warm without overheating and are often odor-resistant, so they’re great for active or travel-heavy lifestyles. Bonus: Many are machine washable, adding a dose of convenience.

Cotton sweaters are breathable, lightweight, and perfect for transitional weather or layering indoors. They’re soft on the skin and great for those who find wool too itchy. Cotton doesn’t retain as much heat as wool, so it’s best suited for milder climates or casual settings. Expect easy care—most cotton sweaters are machine washable.

Blended fabrics combine the best of both worlds. For example, wool-cashmere blends deliver the softness of cashmere with the durability of wool, while wool-cotton blends offer a balance of warmth and breathability. These blends are often more affordable and easier to care for than pure fibers.

Alpaca wool is soft, silky, and hypoallergenic—great for those with sensitive skin. It’s warmer than regular wool but feels lighter, making it perfect for chilly days without feeling too heavy. Alpaca sweaters often have a natural luster, giving them a polished, luxurious look.

The best sweaters for men should strike the perfect balance—tailored enough to look polished, but comfortable enough for all-day wear. Pay attention to the shoulder and chest areas, which should be roomy enough for an undershirt or a button-down shirt underneath, but also not too loose and still snug and slim enough for looking elevated during standalone wear. Sleeves should hit at the wrist bone when your arms are relaxed at your sides and the overall silhouette should be neither too tight nor too loose. A well-fitting sweater not only enhances your style but also maximizes comfort and complements your body shape.

Opt for designs that work across settings, whether it’s a classic crewneck for casual days, a half-zip for sporty outings, or a cable-knit for a dressier touch. A great sweater should transition with no problem from every location to the next.

Between Style Director Christian Gollayan, who’s spent the past decade covering men’s fashion, and me, who’s tested sweaters, jackets, and everything in between over the past five years, we’ve worn enough knits to fill an entire coat check. Together, we pulled on dozens of sweaters in every fit, fabric, and price point to see which ones actually live up to the hype. We wore them to the office, out to dinner, on weekend errands, and through too many cold commutes. We paid close attention to how each sweater fit (flattering or frumpy?), how it felt against the skin (buttery soft or scratchy mess?), how it held up after a wash, and whether it layered neatly without bulk. After plenty of wear, tear, and mirror checks, we narrowed it down to the sweaters that truly earn their keep—sharp, comfortable, durable, and ready for anything winter throws your way.

The key lies in understanding the different styles of sweaters and pairing them accordingly for various occasions. For a casual, laid-back look that you can wear every day, try a classic crewneck sweater with your go-to pants—perfect for running errands or grabbing coffee with friends. V-neck sweaters are ideal for smart-casual or business-casual settings, whether you're at the office or at dinner, since they layer beautifully over collared shirts. (Zip sweaters also work as such, by the way.)

Cardigan sweaters are easy to dress up: layer a button-down shirt beneath a well-fitted cardigan for a sophisticated, professional-looking appearance, or pair them with khakis and tailored trousers to achieve a preppy look. Similarly, turtlenecks exude refinement and work for cocktail and business-casual attire, easily paired with tailored trousers and blazers for a polished, upscale look. For a more rugged, outdoorsy vibe, opt for a chunky cable knit or fisherman sweater.

#4780. The Healing Power of a Post-Divorce ‘Hoe Phase’

Many women use celibacy to process and move on from a breakup, but what if casual sex is the antidote they need instead?

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Zion* was little more than a stranger when he lifted me up onto his lap in one swift movement. His hands were sure, yet soft, as he held my face, kissing me deeply. After a few moments, I pulled back, then looked down, unsure of how to respond to what I could feel was his obvious desire for sex.

I wanted him. But I was afraid I didn’t know how to do this.

Zion was the second man I’d been with since my divorce, but he was the first one I actually liked—and that I wanted to like me back.

Sensing my insecurity, Zion tipped my chin to his mouth and kissed me softer. With my legs wrapped around his waist, he picked me up and carried me to his bedroom. I threw my head back, curls wild, and giggled in a way I hadn’t in over a decade of being married.

As our bodies tangled together, our breathing synced, he looked me directly in the eyes and asked, “Are you ok? How does this feel?” I had never had a man check in with me like that.

“I feel so safe with you,” I whispered into Zion’s ear. It surprised me to know how true that was since we’d only met a few hours ago. I’d been sitting alone at a bar, as had he, and we’d struck up a casual conversation that quickly turned intimate.

I hadn’t felt safe in a long time. Not since sex with my ex-husband had become less like something I looked forward to each week and more like a duty I dreaded.

Throughout our 13-year marriage, I felt like I had expectations placed on me and my body as a wife—my husband’s “needs” often seemed to supersede my own. Consent felt implied. I didn’t think I could say “no” because that might be met with anger or coercive tactics, like begging me over and over until I relented. Each time, my sense of safety and trust eroded.

Eventually, I started recoiling from my husband’s touch because it felt like every hug or little neck rub would turn into him wanting sex.

Naturally, my libido took a nosedive. I thought the problem was me, so I went to sex therapy. But as I started to explore myself in those sessions, I realized I was still sexual. In fact, I was highly sexual. I just didn’t want to have sex with him because I always felt hypervigilant for my emotional and physical safety.

After two months of sex therapy, I asked my ex to sleep in a separate bedroom. Then, I asked for the separation that led to our divorce.

In the early stages of my separation, I was tempted to swear off sex—and men—entirely. This is not uncommon, says Laura Sgro, LCSW, an anxiety and trauma therapist in Los Angeles. “Many women are like ‘screw men,’ because it’s a fear-based response,” she explains. “They’ve learned over time, especially in long-term marriages, to associate sex and intimacy with something that’s not going to be pleasurable for them, with something that’s not really their choice.”

Additionally, love and relationship coaches on social media often suggest celibacy as a way to heal after divorce and sexual trauma. But what if casual sex is the antidote many women need instead?

Once the stress of the divorce dissipated and I settled into my new life as a single mother, I just wanted to have some fun. So, I started leaving my house more often, instead of being wrapped up in “mom duties” all of the time. I went to cute cafes to work, had lunch or drinks at a bar, smiled at men who looked at me, and started conversations with people around me. That’s how I met Zion, and, well, one thing led to another…

Although I liked him—immediately—I wasn’t looking for commitment. Being someone’s partner or girlfriend didn’t sound appealing to me because I’d just escaped all the oppressive gendered expectations that had come with those labels. I just wanted to feel desired and have sex again—uninhibited, no strings attached, exploratory, and pleasurable. I wanted to be free.

Casual sex can be a way for women to take their agency back, says Alica Livingston, a licensed marriage and family therapist based in Texas. “When sex becomes their choice—who they have sex with, when they have sex, what that sex looks like—it can be an incredibly healing and powerful experience.”

It can also be an informative one. Many women don’t know what they like in the bedroom because so much of their sexual experience has been framed around their partner’s pleasure, says Sgro. Embracing casual sex after a breakup or divorce can help women center their own pleasure and regain their confidence.

But if you want to get to know your body better before jumping into bed with someone new, try some solo exploration. “Experimenting with self-touch, even non-sexually, can help women identify what they actually like and dislike,” says Sgro. She suggests touching yourself in ways you haven't tried before—light, firm, slow, still—and rate sensations as pleasant, neutral, or not for you. (For example, you might enjoy gently trailing your finger along the inside of your forearm, but want a firmer touch around your erogenous zones.) Over time, this self-exploration can expand into more sensual territory, like trying toys that offer different sensations or inviting a partner to explore further.

Sgro also recommends women find a hobby or activity that helps them connect with their bodies. “Many women feel disconnected from their bodies post-divorce, and it's so important to rebuild that connection with yourself on your terms,” she says. It can be yoga, weight lifting, dance classes—anything that helps you feel stronger, more empowered, and able to express yourself through movement.

For me, it was twerk classes. The rap music reminded me of the ’90s video vixens and my first “hoe phase” in high school. As a young woman, I had a lot of unsatisfying, performative sex out of pressure to be cool and feel chosen.

This, of course, is the argument against casual sex, and why embracing it often goes against the popular #BoySober and “decentering men” movements. These trends are not only a direct response to the violence women risk by romantically interacting with men; they are also evidence of the humiliating and lackluster dating dynamics we face now—breadcrumbing, micro-cheating, future faking, monkey branching (the Gen Z-informed list goes on).

It’s also true that more women than men experience postcoital dysphoria and regret after one-night stands, booty calls, and casual sexual encounters. But this isn’t just another case of the classic gender gap—it’s due to a variety of factors, not least of which is sexual satisfaction.

But casual sex that is intentional, focused on self-exploration, and re-centers your pleasure can take off the pressure to perform or please your partner, says Sgro.

Now that I was in my late 30s, I was determined that my second “hoe phase” would be all about me and what I wanted. For starters, I wrote down my “Hell Yes” and “Hell No” lists. It was an easy and straightforward way for me to figure out what I liked in bed, what I wanted to try, and what I wasn’t open to. I also used sexting to get more comfortable sharing my desires and boundaries with new partners, which was great practice for having those conversations in person.

For me, having a post-divorce “hoe phase” was exactly what I needed. I started having the best sex of my life, including with Zion. He was the first man I saw myself with post-divorce, but neither of us were ready for a commitment at the time, so our connection only lasted a few weeks. For the next three years, I entertained many casual romantic and sexual connections. Eventually, I realized that while having no-strings-attached sex was great, I love monogamy and would like to get married again. So, earlier this year, I started seriously dating someone else.

Unfortunately, it didn’t work out, and I recently became single again. Part of me wonders if I should have another “hoe phase”? Or, should I stay away from random men until I find my husband?

Sgro says any woman going through a divorce or a breakup should ask herself these kinds of questions—and be honest in her answers. “If you want casual sex, give yourself that permission to explore it in a way that feels good for you,” she says. “And if you’re not ready for that, that’s OK too. No one makes the rules except you.”

So, I don’t know if I’ll continue to embrace casual sex, take some time to explore celibacy, or perhaps return to a past romance. What I do know is that my “hoe phase” opened possibilities—for more autonomy and more pleasure. And maybe even love.

#4777. Toyota updates the 2027 RAV4 PHEV with an NACS port and up to 52 miles of EV range

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 is bringing a few major updates, including an added NACS charge port on all plug-in hybrid (PHEV) models.

The RAV4 was Toyota’s best-selling nameplate in the US last year and consistently ranks among America’s most popular vehicles alongside the Ford F-Series and Chevrolet Silverado.

For the 2027 model year, Toyota added several notable upgrades. The 2027 Toyota RAV4 will be available with hybrid (HEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with available front- or all-wheel drive (AWD).

The biggest change is that all 2027 RAV4 PHEV models now have a built-in NACS charge port with Level 3 DC fast-charging capabilities.

The NACS port is on the driver’s side and lets drivers use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. All PHEV grades also include an 11 kW onboard AC charger.

Powered by Toyota’s sixth-generation PHEV system, the plug-in RAV4 has standard AWD with a combined output of 321 horsepower. The setup includes a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, two electric motors, and a high-capacity traction battery.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 PHEV offers up to 52 miles of pure electric range on the base SE trim. It will be available in four trims: SE, XSE, Woodland, and GR Sport.

Toyota updated the suspension system in the Woodland grade for the 2027 model year with new springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers, giving it 9.1″ of ground clearance.

The Woodland trim adds a rugged look with standard All-Terrain tires, Roof Rails with Cross Bars, and a Tow Hitch Receiver. It also features new all-weather floor and cargo mats.

Lastly, the RAV4 GR Sport trim is for those who want a more performance-oriented, sporty style, with GT-tuned suspension and steering, sports seating, and a standard PHEV powertrain with AWD.

Inside, the 2027 RAV4 includes a standard 12.3″ digital cluster and a 10.5″ touchscreen with the Toyota Audio Multimedia system, plus wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

A 12.9″ touchscreen with a JBL Premium Audio system with 9 speakers is standard on the Limited trim and available on the XSE grade.

All 2027 Toyota RAV4s come with standard Toyota Safety Sense 4.0, which includes safety and convenience features such as Lane Departure Alert with Steering Assist, Full-Speed Range Dynamic Radar Cruise Control, Proactive Driving Assist, and a Pre-Collision System with Pedestrian Detection.

They don't make it easy to find out just what that level 3 charging rate is or how big the battery is. If it's as slow as an old Bolt, could take as long as 20 minutes to charge. If the DC charge hardware is more modern, could be 5-10. Would still be a weird choice, but if you need to stop for a drink of a bathroom anyway, why not?

2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV models are expected to begin arriving at dealerships later this year, while the PHEV models are expected to follow in early 2027.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV starts at $32,300 (LE FWD), and the PHEV version starts at $42,100, not including the $1,595 destination fee.

#4775. Bella Hadid Goes All-In on Colorado With the Purchase of a $5.5 Million Mountain Home

Looks like Bella Hadid is putting down roots in Colorado. On November 10, the Wall Street Journal revealed that the model had spent $5.5 million on a home in Crested Butte, about 20 miles south of Aspen. The news came just a day after Hadid hard-launched her new boyfriend, construction project manager Nathan Lacy, whose connection to the area goes back five generations. According to a statement Hadid’s listing agent gave to the WSJ, she had been living in the region for “several months” before pulling the trigger on her unique new digs, built from two coal miner sheds that date to the early 20th century.

Situated just a few feet from Coal Creek, the 2,000-square-foot residence is complete with three bedrooms and three bathrooms. The sellers built the home in 2001, using two existing structures composed of wood and corrugated metal that had stood on the property for 100 years. The sheds were reassembled over a new foundation, with each wooden plank returned to its exact spot on its wall, according to the WSJ. Antique timber from an old Montana mine makes up the rest of the exterior, while pine reclaimed from an 18th-century Virginia barn lines the floors.

A reverse floor plan was designed to let more light into the upper level common areas, like the fireplace-warmed great room, when snow piles up around the ground floor. Reclaimed warehouse beams from a similar time period to the original structures line the vaulted ceiling, with original iron bolts still in place.

#4774. New Jersey is putting 10 MW of community solar on warehouse roofs

Warehouse roofs are prime real estate for solar, and Faropoint is putting more of that underused space to work in New Jersey. The industrial property owner has started construction on the first of 16 community solar projects totaling more than 10 megawatts (MW).

First up is a 1.6 MW rooftop array at 19-05 Nevins Road in Fair Lawn. Another 15 projects, totaling about 8.5 MW, have been accepted into New Jersey’s Community Solar Energy Program, and nine are already cleared to start construction.

That’s more solar going onto buildings that are already there, with participating households set to get savings on their electricity bills.

Large warehouse roofs offer something solar developers need: lots of flat space. Putting panels up there gives the same building the job of generating electricity without taking up additional land.

Faropoint specializes in industrial properties used for local deliveries and distribution. “Utilizing previously unused portions of our buildings allows us to support the communities where we invest,” said Brian Nave, Faropoint’s vice president of asset management and renewable energy.

Faropoint and its independent solar adviser, SolarKal, expect the 16 projects to generate around 12.7 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually once they’re operating. They estimate the portfolio will avoid about 8,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

Faropoint says at least half of each project’s capacity will be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. New Jersey’s program requires a minimum of 51%.

Excellent. There are so many warehouses around here, it always baffled me that they weren't all covered with solar panels. Next we gotta get to work on all the parking lots.

Faropoint and SolarKal have not yet announced completion dates, subscription prices, or enrollment details for their New Jersey warehouse roof community solar portfolio.

#4772. ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Ben Ahlers and Todd Snyder Know the Power of a Good Uniform

For the label’s latest campaign, the 30-year-old actor takes fall style to Scotland’s Isle of Islay.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

TODD SNYDER makes some of our favorite menswear, and for its latest collaboration, the New York brand crossed the pond to Scotland. The draw? Lagavulin, the distillery that’s been making smoky Scotch whisky on the island of Islay for more than 200 years.

The partnership marks Snyder’s 15th anniversary, with clothes that borrow from Islay’s rugged landscape. Standouts include a brown suede jacket lined in Lagavulin’s own tartan and Fair Isle zip-ups in the earthy shades of the Scottish moors. Pretty great reasons to look forward to sweater weather.

Fronting the campaign is Ben Ahlers. As footman-turned-businessman Jack Trotter on The Gilded Age, the 30-year-old actor knows his way around heritage menswear. Still, these relaxed layers are pretty easy to picture on the streets of New York. We caught up with him about what playing Jack taught him about getting dressed—and which piece he’d bring home.

MEN’S HEALTH: You spend a lot of time in period costumes on The Gilded Age. Has anything from Jack’s wardrobe made its way into how you dress off-screen?

BEN AHLERS: Jack has a consistency to the way that he dresses. As a footman, he had a uniform, and as a young businessman, he has a pretty steady throughline through his looks—a base structure with really well-made clothing and then accents like a tie or a tie pin or a ring that can allow for a sense of creative expression. I find that I like a level of consistency in my own personal dress as well.

More than anything, the greatest benefit of living inside of the clothing that Kasia [Walicka Maimone, the show’s costume designer] and her incredible team make for us every year is this awareness of the way clothes not only make you present to the world but also how they make you feel within them.

MH: Is there a menswear trend from that era you wish more guys would embrace today?

BA: I would love to see some of the creativity come out in menswear and in the accent work, like a tie pin. Some of the tie pins we have on this show are just so well-crafted and specific. The heads of canes the men wore back then also have such an artistry to them, and there aren’t a lot of avenues for that sort of expression in modern menswear. It’d be nice to see that creative voice or risk-taking come through in the subtle accents that we wear in our day-to-day life.

MH: Your role in Death of a Salesman got people talking about your physique. How did you prepare?

BA: For Death of a Salesman, I knew earlier on in the development process that they wanted to go the direction that they did for the top of the show, and so I knew that I was going to be kind of exposed every night. I really tried to go to the gym during the rehearsal process because I knew once we opened the show that it was going to be hard to stay as active—the show was just so draining.

The couple of months up to opening, I really made a practice of five days a week of cross-training, lifting, running, and yoga, and trying to keep my body as nimble and buoyant as possible, because the subject matter and the daily grind of showing up to the theater every day can really take a toll.

During the run, a lot of my focus was on rest, recovery, sauna, cold plunge, diet, stretching, because I’d already built the foundation of the physicality. Throughout the five-month run, it came down to being sure that I was healthy and recovering as best as I could.

MH: What happened between takes on the Todd Snyder shoot that we’d never know from looking at the campaign photos?

BA: Between takes, I had a blast with Boo George, our photographer. He is such a character and one of the best energies on set, and really delivered in the work. The whole crew from Todd Snyder and Lagavulin were so supportive, and it was such a fun little escape for all of us to exist on this island in the most beautiful landscape imaginable.

I really enjoyed getting to know a lot of the locals there. Many of the people there worked at the distillery, and I got to see firsthand how the whisky was actually made. People were so proud to share their culture as well as their craft with the world.

MH: Which piece from the collection would you wear back home in New York, and what would you pair it with?

BA: My favorite piece from the collection is the Todd Snyder x Lagavulin suede stable jacket, inspired by the texture and color of the mossy peat that coats Islay. It’s a perfect fall jacket, and I’d pair it with Todd Snyder’s relaxed barrel jean in khaki, which I think would really pop.

#4771. An Exercise Trampoline Can Make Cardio More Fun. These Are 6 We Like.

Experts share what makes a rebounder safe, comfortable, and worth adding to your routine.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a lifelong distance runner, I’ve had trouble finding low-impact cardio workouts that feel challenging enough when I’m not pounding the pavement. But that all changed when I discovered an exercise trampoline, also referred to as a rebounder. They use a similar style of trampoline to what you used to bounce around on as a kid in the backyard, just with a fitness twist. The result is that the sized-down versions are just as fun, but you also work up a sweat.

Using an exercise trampoline is known as rebounding, and this type of workout is considered a high-intensity movement that’s low impact. That sounds a little confusing, but it basically means using an exercise trampoline will get your heart rate up there while giving your joints a break, something that can be especially appealing for runners. If you’re like me and crave a challenging lower-impact workout that doesn’t include an exercise bike or rower, rebounding might be your new favorite cardio workout.

While rebounding workouts will get your heart rate up quickly, there are plenty of other health benefits to consider, too. A 2024 scientific review found that rebounding can be great for enhancing blood circulation, bone health, and balance. And a small, 2018 study of 18 women found that participants were able to lower their blood pressure and improve their VO2 max—a marker of cardiovascular fitness—on a 12-week rebounding program.

Outside of research studies, Nikki Gnozzio, CPT lists off rebounding benefits of better balance, overall strength, and, of course, more fun. That last part is worth considering, especially if you’ve been struggling with workout motivation or boredom.

Of course, you need a trampoline before you can try this out. According to the personal trainers we spoke with, a rebounder’s tension, adjustability, maximum weight, sturdiness, and size should all factor into your buying decision. Below are six options that stood out.

There are a lot of brands to choose from, but JumpSport stands out as one that’s stood the test of time. “JumpSport has been around since 1996 and is a well-respected brand,” says Melissa Cantillo, an ACE-certified personal trainer and fitness manager at Canyon Ranch. The brand’s mini trampoline line, which includes the JumpSport 530 Pro, popularized the bungee cord system that’s used in many exercise trampolines, she points out.

This trampoline uses 36 adjustable elastic cords for a quieter bounce, with seven firmness settings to help you find your ideal tension. It also uses 16-gauge steel tubing for durability, which is why you can use this trampoline inside or outside (just make sure you bring it back indoors after a good bouncing session to extend the life of your trampoline).

The JumpSport 530 Pro has an extension skirt to protect your feet in case you accidentally land on the cords. The legs are slightly arched at the top to lower the risk your trampoline will tip over. If space is a premium at your place, simply remove the legs and stash your trampoline in a closet or up against a wall to free up floor space.

Plenty of trampolines have features to help you break them down into a smaller size for storage. The Skybound Boogie Bounce Elite takes that even further, with a trampoline that folds in half like a taco and slides into an included carrying bag. The trampoline is relatively small to begin with—it has a 39-inch diameter—but that works in your favor when it comes to storage.

There’s a lot more to love about this trampoline, though. It has a built-in, adjustable handlebar for balance, which is especially handy given that smaller bouncing surface. The frame and skirt are already installed once it arrives, so you can simply snap in the legs and handlebar to get bouncing within minutes.

If you’re looking for workout guidance, you’ll appreciate the free one-month trial of the Boogie Bounce app. It shares more than 100 routines you can flip through. After that, it’s $4.99 a month.

The Stamina 36-inch Mini Trampoline has a petite enough size that won’t hog your workout space. It’s also just over $50, making it the most affordable option in our guide.

In addition to its smaller circumference, it has detachable rubber legs you can pop out to prop against a wall or slide under your bed. Taylor Beebe, CPT points out that the weight capacity is also a bit lower than the other models—250 pounds—but the whole thing collapses for convenience. She also praises the included Müüv app that offers trampoline workouts.This trampoline uses resistance bands instead of steel coils, which likely contributes to its lower weight limit. So, if you weigh more than 250 pounds, it’s best to look for a different model, like the Leaps & Bounds Rebounder. It also doesn’t have a handlebar for added stability, although the 49.5-inch model does.

Many fitness trampolines have removable legs, but some are easier to get on and off than others. While some require some serious muscle and maneuvering to get these in and out, the Leaps & Bounds Bungee Rebounder has legs that just screw into the bottom, creating a pretty flat, easy-to-store surface when you’re ready to stash it away.

This trampoline comes in your choice of 40- and 48-inch diameters. (This is the 40-inch model, but you can upgrade to the 48-inch option if you have the room for it.) The Bungee Rebounder uses adjustable elastic cords for quiet bouncing, along with a durable carbon steel frame.

Leaps & Bounds offers rare perks you won’t see with most other exercise trampoline brands: You can return this after 30 days if it’s not a good fit, and the trampoline comes with a lifetime warranty. While this is minor, it’s still worth mentioning: This trampoline comes in your choice of seven cord colors. Just be aware that if you want to tack on a stability bar, it will set you back an extra $93.

Exercise trampolines generally fall into a category known as rebounders or “mini trampolines,” which basically means they’re smaller than those massive ones kids use in backyards. But rebounders have a relatively small bouncing surface, so you have to be a little mindful about where you jump. The ACON Fit Hexagon Rebounder is 55 inches across, with a 40-inch bouncing surface, which is one of the largest you’ll find. That’s worth considering, whether you prefer a larger bouncing area or just want to build in some added insurance that you won’t accidentally rebound off.

This trampoline has a built-in handlebar that’s adjustable, in case you want extra help with balancing while you jump. The reinforced steel frame has six arched legs for stability. Keep in mind that the legs aren’t removable, just in case you want to store your trampoline in a closet or other smaller space.

The elastic cords allow for a quieter bouncing experience. (The trampoline comes with extra bungees in case one breaks.) This trampoline comes with a 10-year warranty on the frame and two-year coverage on the mat to help protect your investment.

The Sunny Health Springless trampoline delivers the basics at a relatively moderate price tag, making it ideal for those new to rebounding and still figuring out if it’s for them.

This trampoline has a less common square shape, which tends to provide a more consistent, uniform bounce across the entire mat. Since this trampoline is on the smaller side, that’s especially handy for small spaces. The smaller size and removable legs mean it won’t hog a lot of room at your place.

Another perk for beginners? The Sunny Health Springless comes with the free SunnyFit app, which includes rebounding workouts to get you started.

Tension is the tightness and level of resistance you’ll have on the trampoline as you jump. “Smaller exercise trampolines will be more resistant (have higher tension) because they sit closer to the ground, and you don’t want to be tapping the ground with each jump,” says Sydney Sherman, NASM-CPT. “They’re meant to absorb the shock as you land your jump, which is why they’re a great low-impact option for those of us with sensitive joints or coming back from an injury."

Some trampolines allow you to tweak the settings to better suit your needs. An adjustable handle is key (if your trampoline has a handle), Gnozzio says. But some will also allow you to adjust the tension to create a bouncier or less bouncy feeling.

The maximum weight limit for an exercise trampoline will be different based on how it is constructed or the brand. Generally, the weight limit often varies from 250 to 450 pounds. The sturdiness of an exercise trampoline will also vary, but you'll want to make sure it has rubber grip covers for the legs to stay in place (and not scrape your floors) and a handlebar that doesn't easily move for stability.

Sure, you’re already aware that your trampoline needs to fit in your room. But you need plenty of room around it, like a foot on either side, just to be safe. "A lot of trampoline workouts involve arm movements, so you’ll want to have space around you, as well as above you for jumping," says Gnozzio.

While you’re at it, don’t forget to factor in your ceiling height. A minimum 8-foot ceiling height is recommended, according to Cantillo. You don’t need to bounce in a room with an extra-high ceiling since you push into the trampoline more than you jump up, she explains. “Your feet may come off the trampoline anywhere from 1 inch to 8 inches depending on the workout,” Cantillo says.

We’ve continuously researched and updated our guide to the best exercise trampolines since we first published this story in 2021. To find the best exercise trampolines of 2026, we consulted with six personal trainers for their recommendations on elements to consider. We also got feedback from individual trampolines, taking careful note of the pros and cons of each. From there, we researched the most popular, top-rated exercise trampolines, stacking them up against expert feedback and advice. Only trampolines that met our strict criteria made the final guide.

#4768. VisionQuest Reveals Wanda Maximoff’s Return in Avengers: Doomsday and Hallelujah for That

Elizabeth Olsen’s return is a major revelation.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The following story contains spoilers for VisionQuest.

LIKE WandaVision AND Agatha All Along before it, VisionQuest turned out to be among the best Marvel projects to be released in the post-Endgame era. And given that the series was billed as the conclusion to the trilogy that those prior two shows set up, that should come as no surprise. While many Marvel Cinematic Universe movies and shows in the last five years have struggled to figure out what works and what doesn’t—and what manages to resonate with audiences over time—these shows, released over the course of a nearly six-year span, have clearly understood that the recipe for success is pretty simple: a slightly raised concept, and some characters people really love.

VisionQuest took a formula that felt like something of a hybrid of what made the other two shows successful and rode it. Where WandaVision had a super high concept (Wanda turning her world into a surreal series of sitcom references), returning stars (both Elizabeth Olsen and Paul Bettany led the show), and new characters people became obsessed with (Kathryn Hahn’s Agatha), Agatha All Along then introduced the idea of bringing in a vital new character in Wanda and Vision’s son Billy (Joe Locke) to go along with the returning Agatha.

VisionQuest splits the atom by pairing Bettany with a returning James Spader as Ultron (truly fantastic throughout) and introducing Ruaridh Mollica as Tommy, Wanda and Vision’s other superpowered son. The show’s consistently strong, surprising, and well-paced writing from showrunner Terry Matalas—to go along with fun new characters like the Paladin (Todd Stashwick) and E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire)—made it an easy, fun, watchable hit. And it helped that in the end, it came with a punch.

The show continued to expand on Vision becoming human, something Bettany has proven to be brilliant at during the course of his time in the MCU, but it also gave layers to Spader’s Ultron, proving that the franchise can allow some of its iconic villains to stick around and play in shades of moral gray.

By the end of the show, Vision, Tommy, and Billy have made it through the adventure, discovered themselves, and reunited as the family unit we’ve long known they were meant to be. There was just one lingering question: Where’s mom?

VisionQuest asks the question near the end. Elizabeth Olsen’s Wanda Maximoff was the most popular character (and briefly became one of the best villains) in the MCU in the aftermath of Avengers: Endgame; WandaVision was a massive smash, hitting during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and becoming the closest thing to water cooler talk material that anyone could get at the time. Olsen’s performance, nominated for an Emmy, was one of the most important reasons why.

She took a more sinister arc in the following year’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, and—spoiler alert—appeared to be “dead” at the end of the movie. Which puts a serious wrinkle into the possibility of her reuniting with her robotic husband and immaculately conceived sons.

But this is the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and we’re talking about stories based off of comic books. There’s always a way.

Of course she is! Wanda Maximoff is one of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s most beloved characters, and Elizabeth Olsen’s performance as her is truly fantastic. You didn’t think Kevin Feige would leave her alone beneath a mountain, did you?

Sure, it’s been more than four years since we last saw the Scarlet Witch at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, but as the credits scene for VisionQuest (likely a moment taken right out of next month’s Avengers: Doomsday) shows us: She’s back. Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) picks up the bit of mountain she was crushed underneath, and her eyes rocket open in a Jon Snow–esque awakening. “Scarlet Witch, awaken,” Doom says. “Your power will be mine.”

It’s not hard to read into what’s going on here. It’s clear that in Doomsday, Doom is recruiting from some of our existing and most powerful Marvel heroes in an attempt to fuel his own takeover of the world. In the 2015 Secret Wars comic, Doom saves the universe from destruction after incursions (the collision of parallel universes) threaten to destroy everything; the result finds unexpected allyships as Doom takes his place as God Emperor. In that story, Doom’s second-in-command is Doctor Strange… someone we’ve already seen have quite the experience with Wanda (in Multiverse of Madness). Will they wind up allied once again in Doomsday?

The news of Wanda’s return also comes as we learn that her on-screen hubby will also be in Doomsday. “I got to hang out with Paul Bettany, who I love,” Anthony Mackie said in a recent interview, spilling some of the beans.

If VisionQuest was the conclusion of the WandaVision trilogy—and a darn good one—it sounds like Doomsday could feature a full-on Wanda and Vision reunion. And what Marvel fan who’s been along for this ride (and stuck it through to this point) wouldn’t be excited for that? Let’s get the family back together, shall we?

#4767. Segway launches new electric motorcycle that’s so safe it has seatbelts

Segway came to EICMA this year with a surprisingly broad lineup of new electric motorcycles, ranging from high-performance concepts to off-road machines. But perhaps the most interesting of the bunch is also the one that looks the least like a conventional motorcycle or scooter.

Meet the Segway X Cruiser, an electric two-wheeler that takes motorcycle safety so seriously that it has a roll cage and seatbelts.

Or at least, those are among the configurations Segway is showing as it develops the new machine for production.

The X Cruiser is Segway’s attempt to bring more automotive-style protection to a single-track vehicle, essentially asking how much of a car’s safety envelope can be wrapped around a motorcycle without adding another pair of wheels.

From the looks of things, the answer is quite a lot.

Segway says the X Cruiser’s design was informed by automotive crash scenarios, with cage and semi-cage structures, four-direction collision protection, staged energy absorption, and seatbelt restraints intended to improve rider protection. It also gets active safety features including standard blind spot detection and lane change warning.

The company showed several ways that basic idea can be configured, ranging from a more conventional partially enclosed scooter-like setup to versions with significantly more structure surrounding the rider. One of the most striking configurations uses a heavily bolstered race-car-style seat and seatbelt along with protective framing around the rider, while another adds a roof for even more enclosure.

It’s a fascinating approach because motorcycles have traditionally relied largely on the rider wearing the protection. Helmets, jackets, gloves, boots and sometimes airbag vests form the safety system, while the motorcycle itself generally offers little physical protection during a crash.

The X Cruiser effectively flips part of that equation by building some of the protective structure into the vehicle itself.

There’s an important caveat here, though. Segway specifically notes that its descriptions refer to the vehicle’s current design and equipment and do not mean it has completed automotive-style crash certification. Final equipment and certification will depend on individual markets, so it sounds like the company is holding short of making any major certification claims. Still though, it’s easy to see how having what is effectively a racing seat and roll cage surrounding the rider could seriously contribute to better protection in a crash. Just remember to keep your hands and feet within the vehicle at all times.

And unlike plenty of wild EICMA showpieces, this one isn’t merely destined to live under convention-center spotlights. Segway says the X Cruiser has a confirmed mass-production plan, with launches planned for China and Europe between 2027 and 2028. There’s no US availability announcement yet.

Underneath all that protective hardware is a fairly serious electric touring platform. Segway is using its CTB (cell-to-body) battery integration to help improve structural rigidity and battery packaging, with the company targeting nearly 200 km (124 miles) of range.

European versions are expected to feature 4.5 kW Type 2 AC charging, while the Chinese version will offer optional higher-power DC fast charging. The bike rolls on 15-inch front and 14-inch rear wheels wearing Michelin City Grip tires, and riders get a 10.25-inch TFT display along with an optional 55-liter electrically operated top box.

Interestingly, the X Cruiser also incorporates certain two-wheeler intellectual property and know-how licensed from BMW Group, though Segway stresses that it is responsible for the vehicle’s development, integration, validation, production and certification.

The X Cruiser may be the weirdest – and thus perhaps the most interesting – of Segway’s EICMA debuts, but it was far from alone.

The company also unveiled the Segway Orca Concept, a futuristic high-performance electric maxi-scooter concept built around an 800V electrical architecture and a nearly 20 kWh battery.

Segway is targeting up to 300 km (186 miles) of range, a 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) time of 4.5 seconds, and the ability to add 200 km (124 miles) of range in 20 minutes. The concept also features front and rear multi-link suspension, electronically controlled multi-mode damping and a battery-integrated CTB chassis. Those figures are engineering targets rather than promised production specifications, and Segway currently describes the Orca strictly as a concept.

Its a BMW C1 reborn as electric! They were a bit of a cult thing, but underpowered for the weight. Never made it to the USA.

The biggest benefit is not really safety, its comfort.

Then there’s Segway’s expanding X Series, which moves the focus away from urban riding and toward dirt. The lineup includes the Xaber X1000 and Xaber 350, along with different Xaber 300 variants for the US and European markets. Segway is also partnering with Michelin for its Dakar Rally Factory Team, using the brutal rally environment as a real-world development and validation platform for electric off-road motorcycles.

Taken together, it’s quite the showing from a company whose name many people still associate primarily with those funny two-wheeled self-balancing machines from the early 2000s.

Segway has already expanded heavily into electric scooters, e-bikes, go-karts and powersports vehicles. Now it seems increasingly serious about becoming an electric motorcycle company as well.

And if motorcycles with roll cages, roofs and seatbelts are part of that future, things could get pretty interesting… pretty quickly!

Neutrogena is cheap, travel-friendly, glides on clear, and is effective. However, we found it was too greasy for oily skin. This is also Ritchey's new go-to. “As long as you don't smother yourself in it, I feel like it's pretty light for a sunscreen,” she says. “It's a little tacky after going on, but honestly, it was kind of nice—it definitely helped my makeup stick!” It also has a faint sunscreen smell, which she doesn't mind, since it reminds her that Anthelios Melt-In is working. It offers light-to-medium coverage that evens out my complexion without looking cakey or feeling goopy on my face. Problem spots like hyperpigmentation could use some extra love with concealer—Tower 28 makes a sweet one—but I don’t feel insecure if those spots show through with this sunscreen. It took me some trial and error to discover my exact shade, but I landed on the color 40 Silver Lake on my face and use 55 Temescal as a bronzer for a deep golden warmth.

Application is also a breeze—it applies nicely with the warmth of my fingers, but I get the most coverage when using a densely packed brush like my BK Beauty 101 Foundation Brush. Knowing that richer sunscreen shades can be a real let-down, I hit up digital designer Taryn Colbert to give this one a whirl. She uses the color 55 and puts its color payoff and longevity to the test. Tower 28 applies evenly to her bare skin and feels like nothing is on her face. Since she doesn’t have any texture or acne issues, she didn’t notice any splotches or separation with extra oil. I also have oily skin and noticed some pore emphasis on my cheeks after a few hours of wear, but honestly, touching up with oil-blotting sheets and a thin, fresh layer of SPF helps.

While Colbert and I agree with Tower 28’s sentiment that the colors are flexible, it would still be nice to have a wider range of undertones in the tan and deep shades. Still, it’s the SPF that replaces my foundation each summer and one I recommend to anyone who doesn’t want to compromise on sun protection or cosmetic coverage.

Powder sunscreen is the most underrated formulation—and Brush on Block is my favorite. It comes in a tube that features soft bristles that I dust over my face like a setting powder. It’s mess-free, making it ideal for touch-ups on the go. The broad-spectrum sunscreen is also water-resistant, so I can dust it on while poolside without worry.

But above all, it earned major snaps from Dr. King, who uses it on her face and scalp as a dry shampoo hack. Beyond perking up your hair by absorbing oil, it can add volume and texture by coating your strands with fine powders, making your hair appear fuller without sticky residue, says Dr. Goldenberg. So how should you apply it? Dr. King likes to gently rub or massage the powder into the scalp with her fingertips so that it’s not visible, she says.

The only downside? There is only one shade available: Translucent. It hasn’t left my caramel complexion looking ghostly. However, the brand makes other tinted powder sunscreens. I’d appreciate it if this SPF 50 became available in richer shades to accommodate more melanin-rich complexions and anyone with dark hair like mine.

Although it’s expensive, associate style and reviews editor Shannen Zitz has repurchased this sunscreen for over three years. ColoreScience is the only tinted sunscreen Zitz found that matches her cool-toned fair complexion without leaning too warm or too dark. “Tinted or non-tinted, it’s one of the only sunscreens that doesn’t cause acne—and I’m on Accutane—and it feels really nice on my skin,” she says.

Men’s Health associate health and fitness editor Jocelyn Solis-Moreira found success with the shade Medium. She admits being picky about sunscreens and often stocks up on European and Asian brands when traveling because those typically don’t leave behind a dreaded whitecast. However, ColoreScience impressed her after one try.

“With only a pea-sized amount, I saw an immediate difference in my face,” she says. It helped brighten her complexion, masked redness on her nose, and even had friends complimenting her glow. “It honestly felt like a layer of foundation that blended perfectly into my tan skin,” she says. She was so delighted with the results that she didn’t even apply concealer or setting powder. “I had to honestly do a double-take the first time that I was applying sunscreen and not makeup,” she says. “I would 100% recommend this product and will be a regular customer after this experience.”

Colbert was impressed by the lightweight texture but noted it required more effort to use. Notably, she had to wait for it to transform from white to her rich complexion before blending it onto her face. Colbert admits she had to work the sunscreen into her skin to ensure it didn’t look streaky, and that she didn’t miss any spots while waiting for the color to change. Still, she appreciates the overall appearance it left on her complexion. While not her perfect shade match, rich does resemble how her skin looks after a beach vacation.

Although each shade adapts to your complexion, I passed on this one because the limited color range wasn't a good fit for my olive undertones. Still, given the multiple rave reviews from our staff, it’s worth trying if you have the extra funds.

The world of sunscreen can sometimes feel like a catch-22: Either you're stuck using SPF that imparts a gnarly white cast, or you're using one that leaves your skin irritated and sensitive. The Supergoop! PLAY Everyday Lotion with SPF 50 sidesteps both of those issues, according to editorial assistant Katie Mogg. “The lightweight formula melts into my skin seamlessly, all while making it feel hydrated and nourished,” she says. Plus, it offers 80 minutes of water resistance, making it her go-to SPF for my sweaty outdoor running sessions.

Although I prefer a tinted face sunscreen, when I know I’ll be near the water or exercising outdoors I opt for this SPF. Play Everyday is my beach bag essential and for any trips to the park. It absorbs quickly without leaving behind a sticky residue on my body. Supergoop! doesn’t leave behind an ashy finish either. Instead, it blends flawlessly into my complexion.

The only thing I’d change about this sunscreen is the sizing options. There are four sizes, the most of any recommendations this list. However, only the extra large 18 fl. oz bottle comes with a pump. It would be nice to have the flexability of a pump with the other sizes, or at least the standard. But it’s not a true deal breaker, and I still like how slim the original squeeze bottle of sunscreen is and how it doesn’t take up too much space in my checked suitcase and beach bag.

Supergoop! is a favorite among dermatologists and our editors for its super-clear formulas—and rightfully so! This all-over version of the brand's star product—the Unseen Sunscreen SPF 40—does the same thing its predecessor does: it goes on invisible, feels velvety and weightless, and offers out-of-this-world sun protection.

"So many sunscreens have given my skin this heavy, greasy feeling right after I apply them, and on a really hot day in the sun, sometimes that can make you feel even hotter," says beauty contributor Danielle Jackson. "This formula is so light that I almost forgot I even had it on. It really makes you feel like you're not wearing anything."

Aloian has oily skin and easily breaks out, but she didn’t experience any body acne with this SPF. She didn't layer it with other body products, but she was impressed by how easily it spread, thanks to its more liquid texture, which blends into her sensitive areas like the neck. “I love this sunscreen—it doesn't leave any white streaks or irritate my skin. It'll definitely stay in my skincare routine for the long haul,” she says.

Honestly, the only con with this sunscreen is that it’s slightly pricey. However, we’ve been testing this SPF for over a month, and our editors predict each container will last them two to three months before a restock.

Ultraviolet radiation from the sun falls into two categories: ultraviolet A (UVA) and ultraviolet B (UVB). UVA rays cause signs of aging, such as hyperpigmentation, lines, and wrinkles. Meanwhile, UVB rays can cause more serious damage, including sunburn and skin cancer. Your safest bet is to only use broad-spectrum sunscreens to help protect against UVA and UVB rays.

Next, choose either a mineral or a chemical sunscreen. Here’s more insight to help you determine between the two formulations.

They both have benefits and limitations, but ultimately, the best one is the sunscreen you’ll actually use and reapply. As for me? Well, I like both types. However, I typically use mineral sunscreen on my face, so I can head outside immediately after work instead of lingering for the approximately 15-minute waiting period associated with chemical sunscreens.

Broad-spectrum coverage, sunscreen type, and SPF coverage are the big three considerations. But another factor worth emphasizing is other non-active skincare ingredients that will help bolster your complexion. Dermatologist Elyse Love, MD, is a big fan of niacinamide to calm the skin and improve its tone and texture. Also, look for ingredients that support your skin type and goals. For example, if you want to brighten your complexion, you'll look for a sunscreen with vitamin C. If you have dry skin, seek out hydrating ingredients like hyaluronic acid.

When we initially published this story in May 2019, it was a gallery featuring a handful of sunscreens. Nearly seven years later, we’ve seriously upgraded our product vetting process.

For starters, we polled dermatologists about the actual sunscreens they use IRL and recommend to patients. The doctors answered a series of questions about the efficacy, application, and real-world testing experience that helped inform their suggestions.

Next, I evaluated the hundreds of sunscreens in the Women’s Health beauty closet. I also polled Women’s Health and Men’s Health editors about their ride-or-die sunscreens. Our team varies across age, skin type, complexion, budget, and lifestyle. For example, fitness editor Cori Ritchey, CSCS, is a certified strength and conditioning coach and group fitness instructor. She has a no-frills approach to beauty and wants a simple sunscreen that delivers results, which she found in La Roche-Posay.

Clear sunscreens were carefully evaluated. Our team asked ourselves if the clear sunscreens squeezed out clear or were they white or creamy and then blended out without a trace? Associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian and editorial assistant Katie Mogg found success with Supergoop!

Tinted sunscreens were also inspected because I know firsthand what it’s like to try and find your best color match only for it to look ruddy or cool in natural sunlight. With 17 flexible shades, Tower 28 delivers the most inclusive range among the sunscreens we vetted. The hues vary in depth and undertone, and offer light-to-medium coverage.

Whether you have oily, dry, or combination skin, there's something on our list for you. Meet our team’s all-time favorite sunscreens that we’ll continue to rely on throughout 2026.

You’ll want to keep an eye out for certain key phrases on the label. Dealing with sensitive skin? Dermatologist Marnie Nussbaum, MD, recommends fragrance-free and hypoallergenic formulas. She also prefers mineral sunscreens made with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide for sensitive skin because they’re less likely to cause irritation. Acne happens to the best of us, but your best path forward is to use an oil-free and non-comedogenic sunscreen that won’t congest your pores.

#4764. Bunny Williams Never Set Out to Collect Birdhouses—Now a Whole Village of Them Stands in Her Connecticut Garden

Among the apple trees at the edge of AD100 Hall of Famer Bunny Williams’s storied country garden in Falls Village, Connecticut, stands a church with a sensible tin roof; a thatched cottage; a pagoda; a red house flying a tiny flag that she takes for a general store; and a shuttered confection that suggests a Russian dacha. Each is raised high on its own post, finished on every side, painted and weathered like the structures of a settled town—and none has a door you could fit a hand through. It is a hamlet fashioned for birds, assembled building by building, the way real towns often grow: slowly, and without a master plan.

For many years as Williams and her husband, the antiques dealer John Rosselli, combed fields and fairs for Treillage, the much-loved shop they ran in New York City until 2015, the birdhouses kept finding her. They gathered on shelves in the hayloft of her barn. “When I had two, I didn’t know what to do with them,” she says. “Then all of a sudden there were 10.” She decided they had been in storage long enough.

A farmhouse with a side porch crafted by the late Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for fashioning charmingly detailed structures with metal roofs.

An A-frame house embellished with gingerbread trim and decorative brackets

Williams, on a tree stump next to the pagoda. The notch in the base of the birdhouse indicates that it was probably designed to be mounted on a roof.

At that point, Williams and Robert Reimer, head gardener on her property, started the process of reclaiming a long-overlooked point of land. To create space and liberate a stand of existing apple trees, they removed invasive species, then planted oat grass, bird-friendly scrub plants, and fruit-bearing pawpaw trees. To create the neighborhood, she had uniform posts made—tall, “so that you look up at them,” each wrapped with a metal band to deter ambitious squirrels from climbing too high and disturbing the tenants she had in mind. Finally, up went the houses, now totaling 17.

The attraction had nothing to do with value or pedigree. “Most of these birdhouses are sort of folk art,” she says. “They were somebody having fun building an unusual structure.” Not Monticello in miniature, not a replica of someone’s own house, just unknown makers, each with “an eye and a kind of humor,” none of them trying to be perfect. The proof is in the details: the gingerbread scallops on one many-holed high-rise (“somebody had a great time with their little saw”), the thatched-roof cottage she prizes because she has never seen another like it, the weather vane crowning the would-be dacha.

A church with a brick chimney, an oversized cupola, and Gothic Revival design elements.

A rare combination house and feeder that evokes a neoclassical temple

Williams calls this one the general store.

A colonial revival house with a columned portico built by Larry Smith

“It has a kind of Russian dacha feeling,” says Williams.

What she didn’t have was history—the dealers who sold them seldom had any to pass along. The record, it turns out, is often recoverable. “The period from 1890 to 1930 is really the birdhouse’s golden age,” says Jacob Torkelson, an architectural historian and researcher at the University of Pennsylvania’s Stuart Weitzman School of Design, and among the very few scholars in the country studying these objects, whose makers and manufacturers he has painstakingly been identifying, where a name survives. Across those decades, government pattern books encouraged farmers to install birdhouses to reduce pesticide use (the birds would eat the insects), while mail-order companies offered them to homeowners as pure whimsy, not to mention a way of promoting biodiversity in their gardens. Shown photographs of Williams’s collection, Torkelson supplied some of what the dealers couldn’t. He traced one house down to the catalog page: the six-room Bungalow Martin House sold by the E.F. Hodgson Company, which listed the model from about 1917 until the firm closed in 1944. “Birdhouses are these wonderful mirrors to the human condition,” Torkelson says. “They tell us the values that we have as a society or as individuals, in our houses, in our gardens.”

A double porch house also built by Larry Smith

This pagoda-inspired birdhouse provides multiple roosting spots.

An unusual thatched-roof cottage prized by Williams, who has never seen another like it.

Williams isn’t finished collecting. Last May at Trade Secrets, the annual Litchfield Hills garden fair she cofounded in 2001 to raise funds for a local nonprofit domestic violence support agency, she stopped at the tent of Jim Sidon, whose company, Sparrow 10:29, crafts avian-size replicas of real buildings. Sidon, based outside Atlanta, came to the work after retiring from the printing industry. His first architectural birdhouse, built in 2017, was a replica of the 1792 Federal-style mansion in Newburyport, Massachusetts, where he and his wife had rented two rooms as newlyweds. It was Sidon who recognized, in three of Williams’s houses, the hand of his late friend Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for his metal roofs and charmingly rustic details. Williams has asked Sidon to build her something new, though she is still deciding exactly what. Unlike her anonymous makers, Sidon numbers and signs every house. “My hope is that years from now, someone’s searching that out,” he says, “and when they open it up, they’ll see my signature.”

A dovecote-inspired birdhouse offers multiple residences

A picturesque house topped with a prominent weather vane

Drawing the eye like miniature garden follies, the houses rise on poles amid a stand of apple trees from ground planted with oat grass and bird-friendly scrub plants.

In Falls Village, the upkeep routine is minimal: Every couple of years the houses come down, receive a coat of wood preservative, and go back up into the weather. Sidon’s constructions, with cedar exteriors and sealed against the elements, ask even less. His replica of the Newburyport house has stood in his own garden for nearly a decade untouched. “I just hose it off,” he says. None of this troubles Torkelson, a preservationist by training. “These houses were made to be ephemeral,” he says. “They weren’t made to last forever, and they should absolutely be used.”

As for the intended residents? Williams thinks the birds mostly prefer making their homes in the trees, where they carry on, she says, like a symphony orchestra: “I’ve always felt that one of the reasons they don’t live in these houses is the birds think it’s suburbia. But they like the atmosphere.” Come winter, when the woods go bare and the village shows through the branches, Sidon would bet the houses do get used, songbirds crowding in two and three at a time for warmth. Williams can’t say—she has never once climbed up to look. “If they are nesting,” she says, “I don’t want to bother them.”

#4763. BYD’s newest EV is about as big as a Toyota Camry, but brings a lot more tech for $23K

BYD launched the new Seal 07 in China, where it starts at around $23,000. It’s about the size of a Toyota Camry, but brings a surprising amount of tech and premium features for the money.

After introducing the updated first-generation Seal 07 in March, BYD launched the second-gen model on Thursday.

The second-generation Seal 07, which BYD calls the “new choice for a class-leading luxury experience,” is available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains.

BYD offers five variants, including two PHEVs and three EVs, starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery, providing a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

It comes standard with a single rear-mounted electric motor producing up to 328 hp (245 kW) and 269 lb-ft (365 Nm) of torque, which BYD says enables it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 5.5 seconds.

All plug-in hybrid variants use BYD’s latest DM-i system, which features a 1.5L turbocharged engine with 154 hp (115 kW) and a 214 hp (160 kW) front electric motor.

The new Seal 07 PHEV has a smaller 37 kWh battery that provides up to 205 miles (330 km) of pure electric CLTC range. That’s a considerable jump from the 143 miles (230 km) of electric range the previous generation offered.

Thanks to BYD’s latest Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes. To go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

Both versions are 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm tall, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly bigger than the Toyota Camry.

Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s latest cabin design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.

BYD added several premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio. It also offers the most rear passenger space and the largest frunk (160L) in its class, according to BYD.

The Seal 07 debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that can interact with the vehicle and let drivers manage functions remotely.

Higher-priced models offer BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, with a roof-mounted LiDAR available as an option. The setup provides safety and convenience features such as Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

BYD is offering a limited-time “Super trade-in price” promo, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.
